title: Must and can’t: deductions now and in the past
summary: Use must to draw a strong conclusion supported by evidence and can’t to reject an explanation as implausible. Extend those deductions to the past with must have and can’t have + past participle, including deductions about actions in progress.
learningObjectives: Draw strong positive deductions about current situations using must + base verb, be or be -ing.
Express strong negative deductions with can’t, distinguishing impossibility in the speaker’s judgement from prohibition.
Infer likely past events with must have + past participle and reject past possibilities with can’t have + past participle.
Use must have been -ing and can’t/couldn’t have been -ing to infer or reject an activity in progress in the past.

explanation.heading: Must for a strong conclusion from evidence
explanation.body: Use must + base verb when the available clues make an explanation seem almost certain to you. It expresses an inference, not an instruction: If the room is full of boxes, the occupants must be moving. The speaker reasons from evidence rather than reporting a fact directly. Must be can take an adjective, noun or location phrase, while must know, must have and other verbs take the base form.
explanation.example: The bakery lights are on and fresh bread is on display; the staff must be inside.

explanation.heading: Can’t rejects an explanation
explanation.body: Use can’t + base verb when evidence makes a statement seem impossible or highly unlikely. It is the negative counterpart of inferential must: She can’t be asleep; I can hear her talking. Do not use mustn’t for this negative deduction: mustn’t normally expresses a rule or prohibition, a separate topic. Can’t be -ing can reject an action supposedly happening now.
explanation.example: That can’t be our delivery driver; the company says the van has not left the depot.

explanation.heading: Deductions about an activity happening now
explanation.body: To infer or reject an action in progress at the present moment, use must be + verb-ing or can’t be + verb-ing. The continuous form focuses on the activity, while a simple form such as must know describes a state. Choose the time frame from the context rather than the verb alone.
explanation.example: I can hear tools upstairs; the builders must be repairing the roof.

explanation.heading: Must have and can’t have for past events
explanation.body: Use must have + past participle to infer that something happened earlier; use can’t have + past participle to rule out a past event. Couldn’t have is also possible for a negative past deduction. These forms do not describe obligations in the past: they explain what the speaker thinks occurred, based on later evidence. After have, use the participle: left, heard, forgotten or been.
explanation.example: The gate was locked when we arrived; the caretaker must have left early.

explanation.heading: Inferring an activity in progress in the past
explanation.body: Use must have been + verb-ing when the clues suggest an earlier ongoing activity. To reject such an activity, use can’t have been + verb-ing (or couldn’t have been + verb-ing). This differs from must have finished, which focuses on a completed event. Mention a past time or other evidence to keep the deduction clearly anchored in the past.
explanation.example: The floor was covered in paint yesterday; someone must have been decorating the room.

comparisons.title: Positive versus negative deduction about the present

left.label: Must: strong positive inference
left.example: The stage lights are on; the rehearsal must be underway.
left.note: The evidence makes an explanation highly likely.

right.label: Can’t: strong negative inference
right.example: The stage is completely empty; the rehearsal can’t be underway.
right.note: The visible situation strongly contradicts that explanation.

comparisons.title: Past inference versus rejecting a past event

left.label: Must have + participle
left.example: The table was set this morning; someone must have prepared it early.
left.note: The speaker infers a completed earlier action.

right.label: Can’t have + participle
right.example: The shop was closed all day; they can’t have bought the bread there.
right.note: The speaker rules out a supposed earlier action based on evidence.

examples.sentence: With so many visitors waiting, the museum must be popular.
examples.note: Must be draws a strong present conclusion from the large queue.

examples.sentence: No one has a key to this room today, so that noise can’t be coming from inside it.
examples.note: Can’t be coming rejects a present ongoing explanation.

examples.sentence: The lunch boxes are empty already; the children must have eaten.
examples.note: Must have eaten infers an earlier completed action from the result now.

examples.sentence: I saw Rosa on a video call in Lisbon at noon; she can’t have been at our office at the same time.
examples.note: Can’t have been rejects a past location that conflicts with reliable evidence.

examples.sentence: The hallway was full of drilling sounds at nine; the builders must have been working then.
examples.note: Must have been working infers an action in progress at a particular past moment.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The parcel says delivered, so the courier must to be nearby.
commonMistakes.correct: The parcel says delivered, so the courier must be nearby.
commonMistakes.why: Must is followed by the base form be, without to.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She mustn’t be at work; I can see her in the café.
commonMistakes.correct: She can’t be at work; I can see her in the café.
commonMistakes.why: Use can’t for a negative deduction; mustn’t usually prohibits an action.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The pavement is wet; it must rained last night.
commonMistakes.correct: The pavement is wet; it must have rained last night.
commonMistakes.why: A deduction about a past event takes must have + past participle.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The hall was empty at eight; the guests can’t have arrive yet.
commonMistakes.correct: The hall was empty at eight; the guests can’t have arrived yet.
commonMistakes.why: Use can’t have + past participle arrived to reject an earlier arrival.

studyTips: For every must or can’t deduction, name the clue that supports it; the construction expresses reasoning rather than direct observation.
Contrast time frames aloud: The room is dark, so they must be away now; their coats are missing, so they must have left.
Check the negative carefully: can’t be is a present deduction, can’t have been is a past deduction, and mustn’t is normally a prohibition.

exercises.prompt: Nadia has worked since dawn and can barely keep her eyes open. She ___ exhausted.
exercises.feedback: Must be draws a strong present conclusion from visible signs of tiredness.

exercises.prompt: That person ___ the new driving instructor. She is only eight years old.
exercises.feedback: Can’t be rejects the present identification as impossible in this context.

exercises.prompt: No one answered the door, and their car was gone. The family ___ before we arrived.
exercises.feedback: Must have left draws a strong inference about a completed past departure.

exercises.prompt: The gallery was locked from five onwards. The tourist ___ a photograph inside at seven.
exercises.feedback: Can’t have taken rules out the claimed past action at seven, when the gallery was locked.

exercises.prompt: The kitchen light is on and I can hear dishes moving. “Someone ___ (be) in the kitchen.” Use must.
acceptedAnswers: must be
exercises.feedback: Must be expresses a strong deduction about the present.

exercises.prompt: The shop shutters are down and the sign says CLOSED. “It ___ (be) open right now.” Use can’t.
acceptedAnswers: can’t be
cannot be
exercises.feedback: Can’t be rejects the idea that the shop is open at present.

exercises.prompt: Rainwater was on the inside windowsill after last night’s storm. “The rain ___ (come) through the open window.” Use must have.
acceptedAnswers: must have come
exercises.feedback: Must have come uses a past participle to infer how the water arrived.

exercises.prompt: Mia was in Canada throughout Tuesday. “The person in our office that day ___ (be) Mia.” Use can’t have.
acceptedAnswers: can’t have been
cannot have been
exercises.feedback: Can’t have been rejects a past identification inconsistent with Mia’s location.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: She must be working late last night; her office light was on at midnight.
acceptedAnswers: She must have been working late last night; her office light was on at midnight.
exercises.feedback: The evidence concerns a past activity in progress, so use must have been working.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: That can’t be Ava at the station yesterday; she was abroad all day.
acceptedAnswers: That can’t have been Ava at the station yesterday; she was abroad all day.
That cannot have been Ava at the station yesterday; she was abroad all day.
exercises.feedback: A negative deduction about yesterday requires can’t have been, not can’t be.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: You have carried all those boxes upstairs. You must to be exhausted.
acceptedAnswers: You have carried all those boxes upstairs. You must be exhausted.
exercises.feedback: Must takes the base verb be directly, with no to.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The café can’t opened at nine yesterday; the owner confirmed it stayed shut until noon.
acceptedAnswers: The café can’t have opened at nine yesterday; the owner confirmed it stayed shut until noon.
The café cannot have opened at nine yesterday; the owner confirmed it stayed shut until noon.
exercises.feedback: A past negative deduction takes can’t have + past participle opened.

speakingExercises.prompt: Mina has been driving for ten hours and is yawning. State your strong present conclusion in one sentence beginning “Mina” using must be tired.
acceptedAnswers: Mina must be tired.
speakingExercises.feedback: Must be expresses a strong inference from the long drive and her yawning.

speakingExercises.prompt: The official street number is 18, but the paper shows 81. Reject the paper’s address. Begin with “That” and use can’t be the correct address.
acceptedAnswers: That can’t be the correct address.
That cannot be the correct address.
speakingExercises.feedback: Can’t be rules out an identification contradicted by reliable information.

speakingExercises.prompt: You can hear voices and typing behind a closed office door. Begin with “The staff” and use must be working.
acceptedAnswers: The staff must be working.
speakingExercises.feedback: Must be working deduces an activity taking place now.

speakingExercises.prompt: All the biscuits are missing, and the dog is surrounded by crumbs. Say one sentence beginning “The dog” using must have eaten the biscuits.
acceptedAnswers: The dog must have eaten the biscuits.
speakingExercises.feedback: Must have eaten draws a strong inference about an earlier completed action.

speakingExercises.prompt: Max was aboard a flight for the entire office meeting yesterday. Reject the claim he attended. Begin with “Max” and use can’t have attended the meeting yesterday.
acceptedAnswers: Max can’t have attended the meeting yesterday.
Max cannot have attended the meeting yesterday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Can’t have attended rejects an earlier event contradicted by the flight schedule.

speakingExercises.prompt: At nine last night, the neighbours heard music and voices from the flat. Begin with “They” and use must have been having a party.
acceptedAnswers: They must have been having a party.
speakingExercises.feedback: Must have been having describes an inferred activity underway at a past time.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the modal structure and say the complete sentence: “The manager must is nearby.”
acceptedAnswers: The manager must be nearby.
speakingExercises.feedback: Must is followed by be, not is, in a strong present deduction.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences. Fact one: the café sign says closed and the door is locked now. Infer using “The café must be closed now.” Fact two: the manager left the café at five, and it is now six. Infer using “The manager must have left by six.”
acceptedAnswers: The café must be closed now. The manager must have left by six.
speakingExercises.feedback: Must be describes a present conclusion; must have left draws a conclusion about a completed earlier event.

listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker believe about Aria?
choices: She is probably working at this moment.
listeningExercises.feedback: Must be working expresses a strong deduction about an activity underway now.
listeningExercises.audioText: It is almost midnight, and the lights in Aria’s office are still on. She must be working late.

listeningExercises.prompt: Why does the speaker reject the key?
choices: Its size does not match the lock.
listeningExercises.feedback: Can’t be rejects an identification based on the physical mismatch.
listeningExercises.audioText: This key is far too small for the door. It can’t be the right one.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word modal verb phrase immediately after “That”.
acceptedAnswers: must be
listeningExercises.feedback: Must be expresses a strong present deduction about who is at the door.
listeningExercises.audioText: The doorbell is ringing again. That must be our courier.

listeningExercises.prompt: What past event does the speaker infer?
choices: Someone cleaned every tent by hand.
The ground was dry during the night.
listeningExercises.feedback: Must have rained explains the wet ground as the result of an earlier event.
listeningExercises.audioText: The campsite ground was soaking wet when we woke up. It must have rained during the night.

listeningExercises.prompt: Which claim does the speaker reject?
choices: Amir was elsewhere taking that exam.
Amir spent the exam period in the library.
listeningExercises.feedback: Can’t have taken rules out a conflicting past location based on what the speaker saw.
listeningExercises.audioText: I saw Amir in the library throughout the entire exam. He can’t have taken the test in another building.

listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker infer about nine last night?
choices: A celebration has not started yet.
A celebration was probably underway then.
listeningExercises.feedback: Must have been celebrating is a deduction about an activity in progress at an earlier time.
listeningExercises.audioText: At nine last night, I heard laughter and music from the flat. They must have been celebrating something.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word modal verb phrase immediately after “Someone”.
acceptedAnswers: must have opened
listeningExercises.feedback: Must have opened infers an earlier action from a changed state.
listeningExercises.audioText: The window was shut yesterday, but it is open now. Someone must have opened it.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the modal expression immediately after “That”, ending with “been”.
acceptedAnswers: can’t have been
cannot have been
listeningExercises.feedback: Can’t have been rejects a claimed past identity because the speaker knows Oliver was elsewhere.
listeningExercises.audioText: That can’t have been Oliver at the conference. He was with me in another city all day.
